title: Meal Planning
summary: Foods are grouped by physiological function (energy giving, body building, protective and regulating) and by nutrients. The five food group system: (1) cereals, grains and products (energy, protein, B vitamins, iron, fibre), (2) pulses and legumes (protein, B vitamins, calcium, iron), (3) milk and meat products (protein, fat, vitamin B2, calcium, vitamin A, B12), (4) fruits and vegetables (carotenoids, vitamin C, folic acid, calcium, iron, fibre), (5) fats and sugars (energy). Food exchange means replacing one food by another in the same group so that the nutrients stay the same; it makes diet planning easy.

A balanced diet contains different foods in such quantities that nutrient needs are met and some nutrients are stored to withstand short periods of low intake. It has both plant and animal foods, foods from all groups, variety, seasonal foods, is economical and suits the person's taste.

Meal planning is planning meals with adequate nutrition for every family member within the available resources of time, energy and money; it is the 'daily food guide'. Importance: fulfils nutritional needs, makes food economical, caters to preferences, saves energy, time and money and uses left-over food. Factors: nutritional adequacy (most important), age, sex, physical activity, economic considerations (buy in bulk, fair price shops, compare prices, use left-overs), time, energy and skill, seasonal availability (in-season foods are fresh, nutritious and cheap), religion, region and customs, variety in colour and texture, likes and dislikes (change the form, e.g. curd or paneer for milk) and satiety value (feeling of fullness).

Diet modification varies a family meal for each member in quantity (portion size or number of meals; pregnant, sick and old people need smaller meals at shorter intervals, 6–8 a day; adolescent boys need larger portions), quality (change in nutrients, consistency, spices or fibre; mashed dal or khichdi for babies, soft less spicy food for the old) and frequency; or by the food exchange method (1 glass milk = 1 egg = 1 medium katori meat = 1 big katori pulses = 1 big katori curd = ¼ cup paneer; 1 chapati = 1 slice bread = 1 potato = ½ cup rice = 1 idli = ½ cup upma or poha; 1 tsp butter = 1 tsp oil = 4–5 nuts = 10–12 peanuts).

Reference menu: a menu for an adult man or woman with moderate work. The woman's energy is about two-thirds of the man's, so less cereal and pulses but more iron and vitamin C foods (sprouted pulse raita, methi aloo). Pregnant woman: more calories (modified), protein, calcium, iron, vitamins A and C, more water and fibre against constipation and small frequent meals. Lactating mother: needs greater than a pregnant woman; more milk, curd, pulses, egg and vitamin A foods (mango). Infant: mother's milk till 6 months; weaning gradually from 6 months: liquid (6 months), semi-solid (6–9 months: porridge, kheer, mashed banana or potato) and solid (9–12 months: khichdi, egg, chapati); infants need ¼ the calories but more calcium and protein. Preschoolers: high-calorie, high-protein food, mildly flavoured, finger foods. School-going children: energy-rich foods and a tasty nutritious tiffin. Adolescents: high calories, protein, calcium and iron, nutritious snacks; discourage crash diets. Old people: less energy and fat, same protein, lots of water and fibre, soft well-cooked food.

A therapeutic diet is a special modified diet given to a person with a disease to help recovery. Reasons: to maintain nutritional status, correct deficiencies, change consistency and change weight. Keep it close to the family diet, include liked foods and serve attractively. Modifications are in consistency (liquid or semi-solid), nutrient content (increase or decrease) and interval and frequency of feeding (8–10 small meals). Diarrhoea: liquid or semi-solid, low fibre, frequent meals, more fluid (soups, banana, curd; avoid whole cereals, fried food). Fever: semi-solid, high calorie and protein, meals every 2–3 hours. Diabetes: normal consistency, no sugar, six small meals at fixed times. Hypertension: low calorie, low cholesterol and low salt. Jaundice: start with liquids, low fat, small frequent meals. Constipation: high fibre and lots of water.

Diabetics cannot eat rice or potatoes (fact: a little can be taken daily). Jaundice patients should avoid turmeric (fact: fats are excluded for a while but turmeric is not harmful). Crash dieting is good (fact: starvation is harmful; a controlled high-fibre, low-calorie diet is recommended). In diarrhoea stop eating (fact: the body needs food to recover). In fever do not give hot foods (fact: there is nothing like hot and cold food).

objective: State True or False. (a) The frequency of food for a pregnant woman should be increased. (b) One cup of poha gives the same calories as one chapati. (c) Out-of-season food is less nutritious. (d) Food exchange makes diet planning easy.
(a) True. (b) False: ½ cup poha equals one chapati. (c) True. (d) True.
Meal planning is influenced by nutritional adequacy and time available. Support this statement with two examples each.

Nutritional adequacy: a growing child needs more protein and a pregnant woman needs more calcium. Time available: a working mother can cook one dish like paushtik pulao instead of three or four items.
Match the diseases with the therapeutic diets. A: (1) Diarrhoea (2) Hypertension (3) Constipation (4) Fever. B: (a) Low salt (b) High fibre (c) Low fibre (d) High calorie, high protein.
Which four food items can Anita include in her seven-month-old child's meal?
Mashed banana or potato, porridge, kheer and mashed dal or khichdi.
Categorise into liquid and semi-solid foods: sago kheer, soup, custard, khichdi, lassi, fruit juice.
Liquid: soup, lassi, fruit juice. Semi-solid: sago kheer, custard, khichdi.
vsa: List the five major food groups.
Cereals and grains, pulses and legumes, milk and meat products, fruits and vegetables, and fats and sugars.

or: It is a special modified diet given to a person with a disease to help recovery. It is a modification of the normal diet in consistency, nutrient content or frequency.

vsa: Priya is in her second trimester of pregnancy. Identify two modifications in the family meal to meet her increased nutritional needs.
Increase protein-rich foods such as milk, pulses and egg, and foods rich in iron, calcium and vitamins A and C. Give small frequent meals with more water and fibre against constipation.
Explain any two modifications in the diet with one example each.

Quantitative modification changes portion size or number of meals; an adolescent boy gets larger portions. Qualitative modification changes the consistency or spices; babies get mashed dal and old people soft, less spicy food.
A family likes to consume curd daily. Suggest four different ways curd can be served.
As plain curd, as raita with vegetables or fruit, as lassi or buttermilk, and as kadhi or in paranthas and dahi vada.
What is food exchange? Give one example.
It is replacing one food by another in the same group so that the nutrients stay the same. For example, one chapati can be exchanged with a slice of bread or half a cup of rice.
Why should a therapeutic diet resemble the family diet?
Diets based on the daily diet are better accepted. The patient does not feel that he is eating something completely different.
sa: Write short notes on qualitative modification, quantitative modification and food exchange.

(i) Qualitative modification changes the nutrients, consistency, spices or fibre, such as mashed khichdi for babies. (ii) Quantitative modification changes the portion size or number of meals, such as smaller more frequent meals for the sick. (iii) Food exchange replaces one food with another of equal nutritive value, such as 1 egg with 1 glass of milk.
List the factors you will keep in mind while making a tiffin for school-going children.

(i) It should be tasty and attractive, because children skip breakfast and take tiffin. (ii) It should be energy rich and high in protein, vitamins and minerals. (iii) It should suit likes and dislikes, be easy to eat and use seasonal foods economically.
Suggest modifications in the diet of a person suffering from fever (three points).

(i) Give a liquid or semi-solid diet such as soups, juices, milk, khichdi and dalia. (ii) Give a high-calorie, high-protein diet with milk, egg or chicken. (iii) Give small meals every 2–3 hours and avoid fried and spicy foods.
Explain the modification of the family meal for an infant of 6 to 12 months (three points).

(i) Mother's milk suffices up to 6 months, then weaning begins gradually. (ii) Liquids (juice, soups) at 6 months, semi-solids (porridge, kheer, mashed banana) at 6–9 months and solids (khichdi, egg, chapati) at 9–12 months. (iii) More calcium and protein foods like milk, egg and green leafy vegetables are given.
la: How can a person's diet be modified in different diseases? Explain the diet for diarrhoea, diabetes and hypertension with the types of modification.

(i) Modifications are in consistency, nutrient content and interval or frequency of feeding. (ii) Diarrhoea: liquid or semi-solid, low fibre, frequent meals every 1–2 hours with fluids. (iii) Take soups, banana, curd and boiled egg; avoid whole cereals, fried foods and leafy vegetables. (iv) Diabetes: normal consistency, no sugar, six small meals at fixed times. (v) Take vegetables, dal, roti, milk and curd; avoid sugar, honey, jam and cold drinks. (vi) Hypertension: low calorie, low cholesterol and low salt; avoid pickles, papad and butter.
